newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy govt considers confidence vote on immigrants.
newsitem.headline: Italy govt considers confidence vote on immigrants.

text.p: Italy's centre-left cabinet said on Wednesday that it would resort if necessary to a confidence vote to speed passage of a draft law that will allow immigrants who entered the country illegally to remain.

Government sources said the decision was taken at a cabinet meeting in response to a threat by the hard-right National Alliance party to introduce a welter of blocking amendments in the Senate (upper house).
Holding a confidence vote in the Senate, where debate on the draft law was due to start on Wednesday, would sweep away the amendments if it goes ahead.
Thousands of immigrants, many from Africa, Albania and the Philippines, enter Italy without visas or work papers, many on small boats that run them in across the Adriatic or from North Africa.

They were given a chance to regularise their status last November, when the then government issued a decree allowing illegal immigrants already in the country to remain as long as they registered with police.
The decree, never converted into law, has since been re-issued five times but cannot be rolled over again.
The Constitutional Court last month banned the practice by which successive government have re-issued decrees, which lapse after 60 days unless they are passed into law by parliament.
The ruling has forced Prime Minister Romano Prodi's government to put several decrees to confidence votes to rush them into law or replace them by draft laws.
The confidence vote tactic is risky, since a government falls if it loses, though Prodi's coalition has an absolute majority in the Senate and would not be at threat.
National Alliance, part of the main centre-right Freedom Alliance opposition bloc, has long argued that illegal immigrants should be expelled.
One of its senators, Riccardo De Corato, said on Tuesday that the party intended to introduce "a wagonload of amendments" to the draft law to hold up debate.
The party responded angrily to the cabinet's warning of a possible confidence vote.
"It's become forbidden to hold debate in parliament," said De Corato.
